title: Meetings
short: Be on time, come prepared, let others finish, keep to the topic, credit others' ideas, and follow up on what you promised.
trouble: Learners interrupt to be seen as sharp, or repeat a colleague's idea as their own. Giving credit builds trust that lasts.

blocks.html: Meetings are where colleagues share time, the way guests share a table. The courtesies of an interview, being on time, listening and following through, carry straight into them.
Be on time, come prepared, let others finish, keep to the topic, credit others' ideas, and follow up on what you promised.

A meeting costs every person in the room the same hour, so lateness and wandering talk waste many hours at once. Letting people finish lets the best ideas come out, not just the loudest. Crediting a colleague's idea is both honest and generous: it builds the kind of trust that makes people share ideas with you. Following up shows that your word means something.

blocks.name: et-scene

lines.text: Let's start. First, the budget for spring.
I think we could save money by sharing a booth at the fair.
Here's my idea: we share a booth at the fair. That will save money.
Thanks, both of you. Nora, can you look into it?

opts.why: James repeated Nora's idea as his own. "Building on Nora's idea…" would give her the credit.

blocks.title: Interrupted
blocks.q: Priya is explaining a plan when Kofi breaks in with his own idea. What would have been better?
steps: Let her finish; jot the idea down.
When she pauses, say, "Can I add something?"
blocks.a: Wait for a pause, then ask to add.

blocks.title: Giving credit
blocks.q: In a meeting, Sam builds on an idea Ruby raised last week. How can he say it?
steps: He names her: "Ruby suggested last week that we survey customers. I'd like to build on that."
That is honest and builds trust.
blocks.a: Name Ruby's idea first, then add his own.
